title: Biomaterials & Tissue Engineering
description: A partial, application-focused undergraduate sequence in biomaterials and cell-material interactions. Core instruction covers material properties, protein adsorption, scaffold transport/degradation, host-response evidence, and failure; selected tissue-engineering applications connect those foundations to cells, signals, and function.

modifications: Replaced 'initial mass' with 'remaining mass' to make constant fractional loss agree with the stated first-order model.

Linked the four original lesson pairs to outcomes 1–4. Corrected the preserved scaffold-degradation and cartilage-evidence item associations, clarified the tissue-strategy objective to include functional readouts, broadened outcome 4 to include application-specific failure modes, and added direct practice for pore-architecture tradeoffs and cell-source choices. Existing question prompts and numeric keys are unchanged. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added an original comparative primer linking metal, ceramic, polymer and hydrogel classes to surface characterization, protein adsorption and application-specific host-response evidence; added eight formative items and four cards. All tabulated values are synthetic; course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Clarified that biomaterials are the instructional core and tissue engineering is a selected application strand, then mapped the local sequence against undergraduate MIT OCW 3.051J and the selective graduate 20.441J comparator. The title remains, but comprehensive tissue regeneration, fabrication, clinical translation and implant design are not claimed; no lesson, item or card changed.

prerequisites.statement: Cell biology; Organic Chemistry I; Statics/Materials; Transport recommended

outcomes.description: Relate material chemistry and architecture to biological response.
Estimate scaffold transport and mechanical constraints.
Compare scaffold, cell, and signal strategies for a tissue target.
Interpret in-vitro and in-vivo evidence and identify application-specific failure modes.

lesson_objectives.description: Connect surface chemistry to protein adsorption and cell response.
Distinguish bulk properties from surface properties.
Balance pore architecture with load-bearing and fabrication constraints.
Model degradation as a time-varying material property.
Compare autologous, allogeneic, and progenitor-cell tradeoffs.
Map cells, scaffold, biochemical cues, mechanical conditions, and functional readouts to a tissue goal.
Distinguish biocompatibility from an absence of any biological response.
Use case studies to identify clinical failure modes.
Calculate degradation half-life and remaining mass for a first-order degradation model.
Estimate a diffusion release time from gel dimension and diffusion coefficient and predict how size and cargo change it.
Compare degradation and release time scales with a tissue repair timeline and distinguish bulk from surface erosion.
Compute porosity from relative density and estimate the modulus of an open-cell scaffold with the Gibson–Ashby scaling.
Apply Darcy's law to compute flow through a scaffold and identify how permeability, pressure drop and thickness enter.
Analyze the trade-off between porosity, stiffness and transport and evaluate claims that a scaffold's stiffness matches a tissue.
Use Young's equation and the work of adhesion to compare the wettability of surfaces.
Apply the Langmuir isotherm and a molecular footprint to compute coverage, the concentration for a target coverage and the monolayer capacity.
Estimate diffusion-limited protein arrival and evaluate what a measurement of adsorbed protein does and does not show.
Relate a gel's shear modulus to the density of elastically active chains and the molar mass between crosslinks using ideal rubber elasticity.
Estimate the mesh size from the modulus and how it changes when crosslinks are lost.
Compare the size of a cargo with the mesh size to judge diffusion hindrance, and evaluate the limits of the ideal-network picture.
Compute the fraction of bonds cleaved and the number-average molar mass for random chain scission.
Estimate when chains become small enough to dissolve and the mass remaining under a lag model.
Classify erosion as bulk or surface using a critical thickness and evaluate which measurements show degradation.
Compute hoop stress, strain and pulsatile distension of a thin-walled tube from pressure, radius, thickness and modulus.
Estimate the external pressure at which a tube buckles, and when a degrading wall falls below a given load.
Compute how narrowing changes flow and wall shear stress, and evaluate what these numbers do and do not show.
Compute relative viability from an extract test and judge it against a criterion fixed in advance.
Identify the independent unit in in vitro and in vivo comparisons and analyze animal-level data.
Estimate how a fibrous capsule limits exchange and evaluate what each layer of evidence can and cannot support.
Compute the number of cells a construct needs and the number to seed given an attachment efficiency.
Compute the population doublings, expansion time and passages needed to reach that number from a starting sample.
Check feasibility against volume and time, and evaluate how donor variation and expansion limits affect a cell-based strategy.
Summarize replicate specimens by time point for molar mass, mass and modulus.
Estimate the fraction of bonds cleaved, the scission rate constant and the exponential rate of modulus loss from time-course means.
Compare the time courses of molar mass, mass and modulus and state which measurement predicts the period of mechanical support.
Quantify how a measured narrowing changes lumen area, flow and wall shear stress.
Test whether mechanical collapse, a chemical effect or a biological response could account for the narrowing, using the models of the previous lessons.
Design a set of measurements, controls and a functional end point that separates the three explanations.
Compare bulk and surface tradeoffs across metal, ceramic, polymer and hydrogel classes without treating class labels as compatibility rankings.
Select surface-characterization methods for chemical state, topography, wetting and biological response, and state each method’s limits.
Interpret protein-adsorption and host-response evidence for a stated application while separating blood-contact assays, tissue response and causal claims.
Calculate the constant release rate from a membrane-controlled reservoir and identify when zero-order release ends.
Apply the Higuchi model and the early-time Fickian slab solution, including estimating a diffusion coefficient from a release fraction.
Compare release profiles, fit a release exponent from two points, and explain burst release and the limits of exponent-based mechanism claims.

duration.equivalent_structure: Proposed 14-week undergraduate scope only. Biomaterials properties, interfaces, scaffold mechanics/transport/degradation, host-response evidence and failure analysis form the core; selected cell, signal and tissue-engineering applications appear in weeks 9–14. Week 1 links the material-properties primer to material classes, surface characterization, adsorption and host-response evidence; week 6 pairs degradation time scales with controlled-release kinetics; week 12 is a synthetic degradation lab and week 14 reads a failure in a degrading vascular scaffold. The 3.051J/20.441J crosswalk identifies substantial omitted topics. Weeks 12–13 add an optional scaffold-property project with rehearsal practice and milestone self-checks. All activities are open, ungraded practice; there are no graded homework sets, exams or graded project, and workload is unmeasured, so the schedule is not evidence of semester equivalence.

weeks.title: Material properties, material classes, and surface characterization
Protein adsorption: wettability, coverage and the layer that cells actually meet
Hydrogel networks: stiffness, crosslink density and mesh size
Porous scaffolds: porosity, stiffness and permeability
Degradation and release: half-lives, diffusion times and controlled-release kinetics
Polymer degradation by chain scission: molecular weight, mass loss and erosion mode
Vascular scaffolds: wall stress, collapse, compliance and wall shear stress
Cells for a scaffold: how many are needed and what expansion costs
Biocompatibility evidence: extract tests, the host response and the unit of analysis
Virtual lab: degradation time course of a synthetic scaffold; optional scaffold-property project
Reading a failure in a degrading vascular scaffold

modules.title: Material properties at the biological interface

lessons.title: Material properties at the biological interface
lessons.worked_example: For an ideal surface with liquid tension 72 mN/m and solid-tension difference 36 mN/m, Young's relation gives cos θ = 0.5 and θ = 60°. A treatment that raises the difference to 54 mN/m gives θ about 41.4° and greater wetting in this model; neither angle establishes protein activity or cell compatibility, which require separate measurements.

lessons.title: Scaffold architecture, degradation, and mechanics
lessons.worked_example: In a simple parallel load-sharing illustration, scaffold stiffness falls from 80 to 50 N/mm while new tissue contributes 20 N/mm; under the same displacement, combined stiffness falls from 80 to 70 N/mm despite tissue growth. This constructed example shows why both trajectories matter but is not a prediction for a real construct.

lessons.title: Cells, signals, and tissue-specific strategies
lessons.worked_example: For a constructed cartilage target, specify cells with relevant matrix-forming capacity, a hydrated scaffold with a stated stiffness range, a time-bounded biochemical cue, and a controlled loading regimen. Measure matrix composition, compressive mechanics, and integration; a marker alone cannot establish functional tissue. This is an in-vitro design map, not a claim about clinical performance.

lessons.title: Translation, biocompatibility, and failure analysis
lessons.worked_example: In a synthetic case, a degradable implant loses modulus, releases acidic products, and develops a thicker fibrous capsule while function declines. These are separate candidate mechanisms: track wet mechanics and degradation products over time, and characterize host response against matched controls before assigning a cause. No single endpoint resolves the event, and the example describes no real device or person.

lessons.title: Degradation and release from hydrogels: half-lives, diffusion times and matching a repair timeline
lessons.worked_example: t½ = ln 2/0.05 = 13.9 days; 22.3% remains at 30 days; τ = (10⁻³)²/10⁻¹⁰ = 2.8 h for the 1 mm slab and 0.69 h at 0.5 mm.

modules.title: Controlled-release kinetics: reservoirs, matrices, burst and release exponents

lessons.title: Controlled-release kinetics: reservoirs, matrices, burst and release exponents
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic reservoir with A = 3.0 cm², D = 5.0 × 10⁻⁸ cm²/s, K = 0.40, C_s = 8.0 mg/mL and h = 0.020 cm releases 0.0864 mg/h while saturated. A matrix releasing 30% at 1 h and 45% at 3 h has n = 0.37, below the slab Fickian 0.5, so a burst should be checked on a √t plot before inferring mechanism.

lessons.title: Porous scaffolds: porosity, stiffness and permeability, and why they pull against each other
lessons.worked_example: For the synthetic open-cell scaffold, porosity, the square-law modulus and Darcy flow follow directly: φ = 1 − 0.1 = 0.90; E* ≈ 1000 × 0.1² = 10 MPa (and 40 MPa at 0.2); Q = 10⁻¹⁰ × 10⁻⁴ × 10/(10⁻³ × 5×10⁻³) = 1.20 mL/min.

lessons.title: Protein adsorption: wettability, coverage and the layer that cells actually meet
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic 45 kDa protein with a 30 nm² side-on footprint holds 2.49 mg/m²; at 0.3 mg/mL with K_d 0.1 mg/mL it covers 75% (1.87 mg/m²), reached by diffusion alone in 0.38 s; a surface with θ = 65° has work of adhesion 102.4 mN/m, and a concentrated solution fills a surface within seconds, so later change is rearrangement or competition.

lessons.title: Hydrogel networks: stiffness, crosslink density and mesh size
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic gel with G = 30 kPa at 310 K and 150 kg/m³ polymer has ν = 11.64 mol/m³, Mc = 12.9 kg/mol, E ≈ 90 kPa and a mesh of 5.23 nm; the 12 kPa gel has a 7.1 nm mesh that grows to 8.4 nm when 40% of its chains are cleaved.

lessons.title: Polymer degradation by chain scission: molecular weight, mass loss and erosion mode
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic 60 kDa polymer with k = 0.0004 per day falls to 4.5 kDa by day 30 (1.2% of bonds cleaved) while its mass is unchanged, and mass loss begins at about day 34 when chains drop below 4 kDa; the 100 kDa polymer in the lesson reaches 5 kDa at 68.9 days, and its critical thickness for bulk versus surface erosion is 6.7 mm.

lessons.title: Vascular scaffolds: wall stress, collapse, compliance and wall shear stress
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic tube with R = 1.5 mm, h = 0.30 mm and E = 1.5 MPa at 100 mmHg has hoop stress 66.7 kPa and strain 0.044, buckles at 24.7 mmHg, and a drop in radius from 1.5 to 1.2 mm leaves 41% of the flow at fixed pressure drop and multiplies shear stress by 1.95 at fixed flow.

lessons.title: Biocompatibility evidence: extract tests, the host response and the unit of analysis
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic extract with control absorbance 0.85 and extract absorbance 0.57 gives 67.1% viability and fails a prior 70% criterion; five animals per group with capsule means of 66.6 and 64.0 μm give t = 0.42 on 8 degrees of freedom, and a capsule 100 μm thick passes a solute at one fifth the flux of a 20 μm capsule.

lessons.title: Cells for a scaffold: how many are needed, how much expansion that costs and whether it fits
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic 0.5 mL construct at 2.0 × 10⁷ cells/mL with 50% seeding efficiency needs 2.0 × 10⁷ cells seeded, which takes 6.64 doublings from 2.0 × 10⁵ cells (13.3 days at 48 h per doubling and 5 passages at a 1:3 split); the 2.0 mL construct in the lesson needs 1.67 × 10⁸ cells, 8.38 doublings and 5 passages, and seeding all of them at once would fill 17% of its volume.

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: degradation time course of a synthetic scaffold
lessons.worked_example: The synthetic scaffold's mean molar mass falls from 100 to 11.4 kDa by day 28 (0.56% of bonds cleaved, k = 0.00020 per day) and its modulus halves every 35 days while the mass is still 100% at day 56; mass first falls below 95% at day 84, so mass alone overestimates the period of support.

lessons.title: Reading a failure: mechanics, chemistry and biology in a degrading vascular scaffold
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic vascular scaffold whose lumen narrows from 1.8 to 1.4 mm loses 40% of its lumen area and 63% of its flow at fixed pressure drop and its wall shear rises 2.13-fold at fixed flow; its buckling pressure falls to 9.9 mmHg by day 60, a local pH of 7.05 is possible in a poorly perfused wall, and a matched non-degrading control, lumen shape and flow end point are needed to separate collapse, chemistry and tissue growth.

modules.title: Material classes, surface characterization, and host response

lessons.title: Material classes, surface characterization, and host response
lessons.worked_example: In the synthetic comparison, fibrinogen rises from 0.44 to 0.61 μg/cm², a 39% increase, while the separate C3a assay and contact-angle results do not establish overall compatibility or a causal mechanism.

lessons.title: Scaffold project guide: comparing synthetic candidates against explicit constraints (optional, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: For a synthetic candidate with E₀ = 3.0 MPa and a 20-day modulus half-time, E(10) = 3.0 × 2^(−10/20) ≈ 2.121 MPa, and the modulus falls to a 1.2 MPa criterion at t = 20 × log₂(3.0/1.2) ≈ 26.44 days, so the candidate meets that criterion only at horizons up to about 26.4 days, whatever its porosity.

limitations: The four original legacy units remain short primers despite their expansion; the package includes one synthetic-data virtual lab and one comparative primer, and is not equivalent to a full university semester. Tissue engineering is a selected application strand, not comprehensive training in regeneration mechanisms, scaffold fabrication, clinical translation or implant design; see scope-crosswalk.md.

A proposed 14-week schedule exists but is unmeasured and unreviewed. There is one synthetic-data virtual lab and no substantive homework sequence, laboratory sequence, midterm or cumulative final. An optional scaffold-property project guide with rehearsal practice and Case studio milestone self-checks (weeks 12–13) is ungraded practice; the separate project draft stays inactive.

Practice items are short formative checks (two to three per expanded prototype unit and six to eleven per original lesson); they do not demonstrate comprehensive outcome coverage or mastery, and objective associations remain provisional.
Bloom labels and structured prerequisite edges are initial authoring classifications awaiting subject-matter review.
Question answers and solution feedback are intentionally public practice authoring specifications, not restricted exam keys.
Of the 74 numerical answers in this package, 23 require a unit, 6 check significant figures and none checks dimensions; the others accept a number within a stated tolerance, with the unit optional.
Total workload and weekly duration are unknown; former nominal credit values and hardcoded reading times do not establish workload.

All materials, cells, animals and numbers are synthetic teaching examples; this package gives no laboratory protocols or medical advice and says nothing about any real material, device, cell line or person. The formulas are first-order textbook estimates, not design methods.

The material-class comparison and host-response sequence is introductory. It does not cover the breadth of metals, ceramics, polymers, surface-modification techniques, complement/coagulation mechanisms, tissue-specific healing or device standards in the official comparators; its synthetic table is not material-performance data.

The scaffold-property project is optional and ungraded. Its five milestones are Case studio self-checks whose private drafts are never submitted or scored; the rehearsal practice uses separate synthetic candidates and criteria, and no software check evaluates a learner's project calculations or written interpretation. Milestone weeks are planning suggestions, not measured workload or deadlines.
intentionally_omitted: Graded assessments, an activated integrative project and a laboratory sequence are not authored yet (one synthetic-data virtual lab exists); the original lessons extend a partial package.
Detailed surface-analysis theory, comprehensive immune signaling, broad device-class coverage and graded laboratory or exam assessment remain outside this bounded primer.
